newsitem.title: UK: New yen surge seen jangling emerging market nerves.
newsitem.headline: New yen surge seen jangling emerging market nerves.

text.p: The Japanese yen's renewed surge this week may have jangled the nerves of investors in emerging markets around the globe even as shock waves from the initial yen move in May still reverberate, analysts said.
There are a number of mitigating circumstances this time around and any ripple effects may be more selective, strategists say.
Yet, another relentless rise of the yen through key levels like 110 to the dollar could well cause another serious distortion to global capital movement.
The Czech crown and Thai baht, the main casualties from last month's capital shift, were steady to firmer on Wednesday despite the yen move as the focus remained on domestic issues.

"The impact of the yen move on the huge overhang of short yen positions is a problem for these markets but it's not a blanket issue any more and people will probably be more selective this time around," said Nick Douch, economic and corporate risk adviser at BZW markets division.
The yen's rise of more than 12 percent against the dollar and 10 percent against the German mark in May, however, was highly correlated with a run on both the baht and crown.
After a brief period of stability, the yen has extended its gains this week to seven-month highs against the dollar and 21-month highs on the mark.

Analysts said the link between the two was at least partly to do with growing fears of a rise in Japanese interest rates. This would raise the cost of yen-based borrowing, extensively in recent years to fund speculative high-yield positions in riskier developing markets of South-East Asia and Eastern Europe.

"The lockstep drop in December euroyen futures and Czech crown last month was unlikely to have been just coincidence and there's a risk this could well return as a factor," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro.

However, Norfield said the sheer size of the yen's gains since May 1 could diffuse the overseas contagion in the short-term by taking pressure off Japanese authorities to raise interest rates. This support would only be short-lived, he said.
Euroyen futures, for example, rose today as a result of a market belief that monetary policy has seen a net tightening as a result of the yen rise.

Yet, other reasons were also cited for the yen/baht/crown correlation - such as the liquidation of high-yield positions by speculative hedge funds in order to pay margin calls on suddenly loss-making short-yen trades.

"There are a lot of casualties left high and dry in dollar/yen and there is a risk that investments in more peripheral markets will be cut to offset these huge losses in yen," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.
Growing bullishness about the prospects for Japanese stocks is one way of illustrating the shift in preferences, said traders.
The relative power of central bank regimes should be a key factor in assessing the vulnerability to any contagion, however.

Douch at BZW said the Thai central bank restrictions on offshore access to baht funding has hamstrung speculation there, for example, where yen-based positions were most prevalent. This has effectively created a two-tier market where many overseas speculators have suffered severely.

Regional central bank accords, meantime, would also likely see powerful reserve-rich central banks like the Bank of Japan or Bank Negara come to the aid of the Thais in the event of another severe crisis, said analysts.
The power of central banks in these less developed markets is often underestimated, they said.

The Czech central bank's reversion to a managed flotation of the crown on May 26 and an increasingly shaky political environment in the Czech Republic make it more vulnerable to international capital shifts, traders said.
Moreover, Douch at BZW said there is a particularly harsh effect on borrowers in yen from the sudden rise of the currency.

A liberalisation of Japanese markets over the past couple of years has seen a wave of foreign borrowers in so-called Samurai bonds - which are yen-denominated bonds issued domestically in Japan by foreign investors.
The rise of the yen will have seriously raised the cost of borrowing for issuers who sold these bonds over the past six months -- many of whom were sovereign borrowers from developing markets.

As the proceeds of these bonds were most likely traded for dollar reserves, the shift in the yen may well see a scramble to rebalance these reserve portfolios and see an exaggeration of the dollar/yen slump.
